Samuel Barber was an American composer born in 1910 who lived until 1981. He was one of the most celebrated classical figures of the twentieth century, known for orchestral, choral, and dramatic music. What set him apart was his commitment to deeply expressive, lyrical, and neo-Romantic language. While his contemporaries embraced experimental atonality and avant-garde systems, Barber remained devoted to the emotional power of traditional harmony.

His signature work is the Adagio for Strings, composed in 1936. Originally the slow movement of his String Quartet Opus 11, it was later arranged for string orchestra and premiered by conductor Arturo Toscanini. It has since become the definitive classical elegy, played at memorials and in films like Platoon, serving as a universal anthem for grief and public mourning.

Barber wrote many other significant works. Knoxville: Summer of 1915 is a lush, nostalgic work for soprano and orchestra setting a James Agee poem about a peaceful summer evening in Tennessee. His Hermit Songs, a cycle of ten songs from 1953, sets marginalia and poems by anonymous Irish monks from the eighth to thirteenth centuries, famously premiered by soprano Leontyne Price with Barber at the piano. The Violin Concerto Opus 14 from 1939 is a brilliant three-movement work with intensely lyrical outer movements and a final presto of perpetual motion that demands extraordinary technical skill.

Barber also achieved success in opera. His first opera, Vanessa, premiered in 1958 with a libretto by his lifelong partner Gian Carlo Menotti and won the Pulitzer Prize for Music. His second opera, Antony and Cleopatra, was commissioned for the opening of the new Metropolitan Opera House at Lincoln Center in 1966. Regrettably, the premiere was disastrous and over-produced, sending Barber into a deep depression and creative isolation.

Throughout his life, Barber remained a titan of mid-century American music, championing the lush neo-Romantic language that defined his distinctive emotional voice.
